title: In the Drops: Uber-wide Reserve gravel wheels, classy Shimano shoes, a posh Berk saddle and speedy Conti tyres

In the Drops: Uber-wide Reserve gravel wheels, classy Shimano shoes, a posh Berk saddle and speedy Conti tyres

It hasn’t been the busiest week on Cyclist.co.uk but what we’ve lacked in quantity we’ve made up for in quality and variety – there’s been something for everyone.

Fans of pro racing got this week’s Pro Log and a round up of the Vuelta a España’s second week, for the history buffs we recounted how Stephen Roche won his Triple Crown, then there was plenty for the tech nerd as well: an explainer on hookless, a showdown between three of the best road race bikes, reviews of Tailfin’s Speedpack and some solid DT Swiss wheels, plus news of Enve’s latest Melee race bike.

We’ve also got a competition with wheel brand Scribe to win a pair of its Gravel Ultra wheels, which you can enter here.

Topping things off, we have the latest instalment of In the Drops weekly product round-up. Enjoy.

Reserve 48|53 GR wheels

Ever since Zipp shook things up back in 2024 with the launch of its then-wild 303 XPLR design (though 3T was truly the first in the space with its Discus 45|40 model), aero gravel wheels with extra-wide rims have become a common addition to the line-up every wheel brand worth their salt.

The 30mm internal, 44mm internal rim dimensions of Reserve’s 48|53 GR wheels undoubtedly qualify the model to be part of the trendy crowd, but the timing of their release means they enter a busy category.

The 48|53 wheels have a couple of features that help make them distinct from rivals, however. First is the staggered depth: Reserve’s wheels are designed around the brand’s ‘Turbulent Aero’ concept, where rims have been designed around wind conditions that Reserve have determined as accurate in the real-world, based on a series of measurements taken on actual roads.

That explains the 48mm deep front, which is slightly shallower to make the wheel less susceptible to crosswind instability, paired with the 53mm rear, which is deeper to encourage smoother airflow.

The second trick up the wheels’ sleeve is their ‘hollow hook’ design. Generally, the bead hook portion of the rim is solid, which when a wheel has wide bead hooks as the 48|53 GR wheels do, can lead to significant weight gain. Reserve has used special moulds however to ensure the bead hook area is hollow and the rim remains light.

Indeed, claimed weights’ are competitive – just 1,433g with a DT Swiss 180 hubset and 1,528g with a DT 350 hubset. Prices are keen too, at £2,399 and £1,599 respectively.

Shimano RX710 shoes

Shimano’s new RX710 gravel shoes adopt a familiar position in the brand’s product line up, by adopting several features from the top-line S-Phyre RX910 shoes but toning them down to decrease cost and increase versatility.

Overall looks, closure arrangement and construction remains similar, but a good example of Shimano’s approach is in the RX710’s sole. It steps down from a full carbon plate to a nylon composite that gets a carbon-reinforced midsole.

Stiffness duly steps down from 12/12 to 9/12 on Shimano’s arbitrary scale, but this reduces cost (the RX710s are £269.99 versus the RX910’s £369.99), won’t significantly affect power transfer, and likely bumps up comfort to boot by making them easier to walk in.

The outsole largely mirrors the S-Phyre’s widely-spaced nob arrangement and the innovative ‘Pontoon’ cleat system to ensure secure connection with the pedal body.

The RX701’s upper is made from a similar synthetic leather for comfort and durability, but the Boa dials reduce from Li2s to the single-direction adjustment of the L6Z models.

The RX710s come in three colours and the size range is impressive, with standard, wide and narrow fits available, along with half sizes.

Berk Lupina Monocoque Open saddle

Berk Composites’ most premium and lightest saddle – weighing a claimed 125g – may be on the pricy side, but that’s because it required investment into specialist tooling to create.

Rather than fixing separate rails into a main chassis, Berk moulds the entire Monocoque Open from carbon in one piece. Berk says the resultant product is lighter and stronger than regular carbon saddles but also gives it the ability for additional flex in the front region.

‘It’s made using resin transfer moulding, where dry carbon fibres are placed in a special mould that allows resin to be injected under heat and pressure,’ says Jure Berk, one of the company’s founders. ‘This lets us use stiffer fibres for the saddle rails and more flexible fibres on the saddle shell for comfort.’

Continental Terra Competition tyres

Because the size of gravel tyres continues to rise, when it comes to traction width is increasingly being used as a proxy for tread. As such, tread patterns are becoming more minimal and off-road tyres are getting faster. Continental’s new Terra Competitions are a great example: they’re said to be the brand’s fastest ever gravel tyre.

‘Their sleek chevron tread makes them 17% faster than our previous race tyre, the Terra Speed,’ says Continental’s gravel product manager, Alexander Haenke. ‘They’re now fast enough that riders don’t have to choose between road speed and off-road capability.’

The Terra Competitions will be offered in two casings – burlier ‘trail’ and more supple ‘race’ – and three widths 35mm, 40mm and 45mm.
